criteria.name: Introduction: mission concept and rationale - Include the following required information: • What is the spacecraft's primary mission? • Why is the mission needed? • How many spacecraft are used and why? • Who are the users (operator and customers)?
criteria.reasoning: The mission concept is clearly explained with a well-justified rationale focusing on coral bleaching in the Great Barrier Reef. The choice of a single spacecraft, the primary mission payload (fluid lensing), and the intended operators/customers are all clearly defined.

evidence.quote: Thus, only one satellite is required. This also just allows for simplicity in communications, reduces cost, and requires less time to build and launch.
The proposed satellite would likely be used by governmental and science agencies (e.g. CSIRO, BOM) for research and/or education.

criteria.name: Main body: mission design - Present a summary of the mission design using software and/or hand calculations as appropriate - Include relevant screenshots and software files (in the main body of the report and/or appendix) - Include the following information: • Where it will launch from, and using which launch vehicle? Why did you choose this option? • What type of orbit will you use? What are its characteristics and orbital elements? • Will you need to perform any orbital maneuvers? • Which ground control facilities will you use? • How often will your spacecraft be able to communicate with ground control? • How long will the mission last, and what are your plans for EOL?
criteria.reasoning: All major mission design elements are addressed: launch vehicle/site trade-offs, orbital elements for SSO, ground facility access statistics, and EOL disposal. However, quantitative design for the drag sail and payload resolution vs. swath hand calculations are lacking, and the EOL discussion contains an incomplete sentence.

evidence.quote: The proposed satellite will thus use the Vega E rocket as a launch vehicle – launched from the Guiana Space Centre Spaceport.
Specifically, an altitude of 600km requires a mean inclination of 97.7924^{\circ} for the satellite to remain sun-synchronous.
The most promising alternative is a ‘drag sail’ – a drag-enhancing deorbit device that deploys at the EOL.

criteria.name: Conclusion
criteria.reasoning: The conclusion concisely summarises the mission architecture, reiterating the launch strategy, sun-synchronous orbit selection, ground station choice, and expected benefits to the Great Barrier Reef.

evidence.quote: The initial problem of not catching coral bleaching events in time can be minimised, if not solved, by the initiation of the ZYZZsat in 2025.

criteria.name: Report presentation
criteria.reasoning: The report structure is readable, but presentation has notable flaws: figures and tables lack standard numbering and captions (e.g., 'Figure 1', 'Table 1'), reference [6] uses Wikipedia against explicit instructions, citation [10] has formatting errors, and a sentence is cut off mid-thought.

evidence.quote: It acts like a regular sail, utilising a large surface area to ‘ and is suitable for low-earth orbit altitudes [10].

technical_issues.issue: Incomplete sentence: 'utilising a large surface area to ‘ and is suitable for low-earth orbit altitudes [10].'
Reference [6] cites Wikipedia directly, violating prompt instructions.
Access report table contains a duplicated entry for Access 14 and 15 with identical timestamps and duration.
Payload imaging resolution, swath width, and optics focal length are discussed qualitatively without supporting optical hand calculations.

overall: A solid, well-conceived preliminary mission design that clearly addresses all space segment aspects for monitoring the Great Barrier Reef. However, presentation suffers from uncaptioned/unnumbered figures and tables, an incomplete sentence in the EOL section, reliance on Wikipedia, and a lack of detailed hand calculations or attached scenario files.

feedback.summary: You developed a well-conceived preliminary space mission design targeting Great Barrier Reef monitoring. You clearly articulated the operational rationale, orbit, launch vehicle, and ground station selection. To elevate your report to an exemplary engineering standard, reinforce your technical narrative with explicit hand calculations (such as optical resolution and drag-sail sizing) and refine document formatting to ensure professional figure captions, verified data tables, and scholarly referencing throughout.

criteria.C1: In the Introduction, you clearly defined the mission's primary objective—monitoring coral bleaching with fluid lensing—and justified the single-satellite architecture and stakeholders (CSIRO, BOM). To consolidate top-tier performance, integrate more peer-reviewed literature and explicit baseline requirements into your operational rationale.
criteria.C2: You addressed all major design areas, including your SSO selection in "Orbit" and the Vega E trade-off in "Launch". To reach the top of the Accomplished band, support qualitative payload statements with quantitative hand calculations (e.g. swath width, resolution, drag-sail area) and verify simulation data tables to remove duplicate rows.
criteria.C3: Your "Conclusion" effectively synthesises the core architecture, connecting the sun-synchronous orbit and ground station choices directly back to the Great Barrier Reef monitoring goals. To achieve full marks, incorporate a concise quantitative summary of your key engineering parameters alongside your narrative summary.
criteria.C4: To reach Accomplished, ensure all visual elements include standard numbering and descriptive captions (e.g. "Table 1"). Conduct a thorough proofreading pass to eliminate truncated text—such as the incomplete sentence in "Mission Duration & EOL"—and replace non-standard citations like Wikipedia with formal aerospace literature.

next_steps: Include supporting hand calculations in "Orbit" and "Mission Duration & EOL" to quantitatively verify optical payload resolution, swath width, and the required drag-sail surface area for deorbiting.
Add formal captions and numbers to all figures and tables, ensuring in-text cross-referencing and removing duplicated data rows from the ground access table.
Replace non-academic references (such as Reference [6]) with authoritative spaceflight or agency sources, and proofread to resolve incomplete sentences.
